newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech coalition appears united ahead of key vote.
newsitem.headline: Czech coalition appears united ahead of key vote.

text.p: The Czech governing coalition appeared unified on Tuesday ahead of a confidence vote in parliament where the fate of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his government's economic programme hung in the balance.
The issue was expected to be at the top of the agenda when the lower house began meeting on Tuesday at 2.00 p.m. (1200 GMT), though political wrangling was likely to delay a vote for several days.
Klaus's three-party, centre-right coalition controls only 100 seats in the 200-seat parliament and even members of the government have been driving hard bargains for their support.

But a key late-night meeting on emergency budget cuts brought the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) on side, and looked likely to shore up the coalition, which has appeared close to breaking up several times in recent weeks.
The leader of the KDU-CSL was reported by CTK news agency as being content with the deal in spite of a decision not to postpone deregulation of energy prices and rents.
Josef Lux had wanted a postponement of the deregulations, planned for July 1, to soften the impact of budget cuts which he had insisted upon to balance the budget.
"If parliament does not decide otherwise, then the deregulations will go ahead," Lux was quoted by CTK as saying.
After more then seven hours of negotiations lasting into the early hours of Tuesday, the government agreed to cut 20 billion crowns ($621 million) from the 1997 state budget.

The attitude of KDU-CSL, which has openly criticised Klaus's style of government and has not ruled out going into opposition with the Social Democrats (CSSD), was widely seen as the decisive factor for Klaus's fate in the confidence vote.
Analysts say the vote will be very close, but expect Klaus to survive with a razor-thin majority.
Klaus called the confidence vote last week after two weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets.
Speculators, alarmed at widening current account and trade deficits and growing political uncertainty, sold the crown, leading the central bank to float the currency on May 27.
Coalition leaders the next day agreed on a sweeping cabinet reshuffle and on the austerity programme, which called for budget cuts totalling some 20 billion crowns and wage freezes.
If Klaus loses the vote, he will be obliged under the constitution to step down, Prague-based political analyst Jiri Pehe said.
If President Vaclav Havel were then unable to broker a workable government, an early election would be called. The next general election is not due until early in the year 2000.
Klaus called the vote partly to spike the guns of CSSD leader Milos Zeman, who had planned to put forward a vote of no confidence at a session of parliament beginning on July 1.
